claims.text: A hybrid first-principles and machine-learning model will predict transport properties of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than standard defect-free analytical models.
The claimed accuracy advantage applies in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed model will correct predictions for defect scattering and oxygen-induced imperfections.
The approach is intended for nominally pure bulk HfNbTaTiZr and material containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Quantum effects and defect-induced scattering are significant from 0 to 200 K.
Thermal fluctuations and oxygen-related defect scattering dominate from 300 to 1200 K.
Defects and oxygen-associated impurity clusters alter electron and phonon scattering relative to an ideal defect-free crystal.
Training a correction module on experimental and defect-inclusive simulation data will make predictions better reflect the real microstructural state.
Accounting for the real microstructural state will improve predicted transport properties.
The hybrid model will have a lower mean absolute error for electrical-conductivity predictions than perfect-crystal models.
Defect-free analytical predictions typically deviate from experiments when defects or impurities such as 1 wt.% oxygen are present.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing oxygen at levels up to approximately 1 wt.%.
The model's stated temperature applicability is limited to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Use beyond the stated oxygen concentrations or temperature intervals may require model modifications.
Preliminary evidence suggests that the proposed approach improves accuracy.
The magnitude of error reduction across different defect distributions and impurity levels remains unverified.
Failure to reduce mean absolute error by at least 10% relative to a defect-free analytical model in either temperature regime is proposed as a falsifying result.
